canberra.title: Man’s condition ‘up in the air’ after alleged serious assault by dating app match
canberra.snippet: A man remains in a serious condition in hospital after allegedly being attacked by his dating app match. It is understood the two men mat...
canberra.content:
24 September 2026

Two men allegedly matched over the dating app Grindr before one seriously assaulted the other. Photo: Albert McKnight.

A man remains in a serious condition in hospital after allegedly being attacked by his dating app match.

It is understood the two men matched over the Grindr app before the alleged victim was left with serious head injuries that saw him taken to hospital.

An ACT Policing spokesperson said the pair allegedly arranged to meet at a home in south Canberra on Tuesday (22 September) after matching.

Later in the evening, the 19-year-old alleged attacker, who is originally from the NSW Far South Coast but Region has not named for the time being, allegedly seriously assaulted the other man before demanding money.

The 19-year-old then allegedly forced him to drive to several locations around the ACT to try to withdraw cash.

“During the incident, the victim attempted to escape the car, but the man reversed the vehicle while he was opening the door, preventing him from leaving,” the police spokesperson alleged.

“He eventually let the victim out in Kaleen where he was able to call for help.”

The spokesperson alleged officers soon found the car in the ACT and arrested the 19-year-old while he was sitting in the driver’s seat.

He briefly appeared in the ACT Magistrates Court on Thursday (24 September) where his lawyer, CODA Criminal Law’s Peter Woodhouse, told the court the condition of the alleged victim was currently “up in the air”.

He said the alleged victim remained in hospital and one of his injuries was a suspected brain hemorrhage.

This is a type of life-threatening brain injury.

Mr Woodhouse recommended his client be taken to hospital for a mental health assessment, and Special Magistrate Lucinda Wilson ordered this assessment to take place.

This means the 19-year-old will return to court in the future to apply for bail.

While the court heard he could live with family if released from custody, the prosecutor said his office would oppose any bail application.

The 19-year-old will be charged with recklessly inflicting grievous bodily harm and choking when he returns to court, but the police spokesperson also said the investigation was continuing and further charges were being considered.

Region will not name the 19-year-old while the mental health assessment takes place.

canberra.title: Lengthy car chase spans Queanbeyan to ACT before alleged driver does a runner
canberra.snippet: A car chase continued through NSW, the ACT and then back again before police finally arrested the alleged driver when he tried to run awa...
canberra.content:
24 September 2026

24 September 2026

A 22-year-old man has been arrested after a lengthy car chase between NSW and the ACT. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

A car chase continued through NSW, the ACT and then back again before police finally arrested the alleged driver when he tried to run away from them on foot.

A NSW Police spokesperson said officers were on patrol in Crestwood, Queanbeyan, around 2 am on Thursday (24 September) when they tried to stop a Kia hatchback.

A pursuit was initiated when the driver allegedly refused to pull over and the ensuing car chase continued on Kendall Avenue North before turning onto Canberra Avenue and entering the ACT.

Officers with ACT Policing took over the chase through the suburbs of Tralee, Hume and Tuggeranong before turning onto Lanyon Drive where the car re-entered NSW at Jerrabomberra.

NSW officers re-engaged, continuing the pursuit through the suburbs of Jerrabomberra Heights, Karabar and the Queanbeyan CBD before the driver went back to the ACT.

Ultimately, police successfully deployed road spikes on Yass Road, near the intersection of Sutton Road, and the car came to a stop on Crawford Street, Queanbeyan.

The accused driver, a 22-year-old man, allegedly ran from the car before he was arrested after a chase on foot.

“The man was searched and officers allegedly located and seized a flick knife,” the police spokesperson said.

“During a subsequent search of the vehicle, officers allegedly located [and] seized a large sword, gloves and balaclavas.”

The man was charged with police pursuit, driving while disqualified and having custody of a knife in a public place.

He was refused bail to face the NSW Local Courts on Thursday.

canberra.title: Developer licensing concession aims to boost homebuyer protection
canberra.snippet: The ACT property industry has welcomed a last-minute concession in the new developer licensing scheme before it becomes mandatory from 1 ...
canberra.content:
Responsibility for defects in multi-unit developments has long been contentious. Photo: Michelle Kroll.

The ACT property industry has welcomed a last-minute concession in the new developer licensing scheme before it becomes mandatory from 1 October.

The key change relieves company directors of their liability for serious defects if they take out a latent defects insurance (LDI) policy that protects future building owners for 10 years.

But Master Builders ACT says action should focus on preventing defects, not adding another cost to housing construction.

LDI, known as decennial liability insurance in other jurisdictions, is not mandatory yet, but Planning Minister Chris Steel said the government was looking to make it so for apartment buildings.

The change, one of several amendments to the developer licensing legislation introduced into the Legislative Assembly on Thursday, is designed to encourage developers to take out LDI.

Other amendments aim to boost the number of missing middle housing developments by providing for a single licence to be attached to a project.

The Property Council said the government had acknowledged major flaws identified by industry when the licensing scheme was proposed.

ACT & Capital Region Executive Director Ashlee Berry said the amendments were a significant step in the right direction.

“We’re pleased the government has listened to us, but let’s be clear, when you’ve pushed an industry off the edge of a cliff, providing a parachute is better than nothing, but it would have been far better not to push it off in the first place,” she said.

The Property Council had long been concerned about how the licensing regime would operate in practice and its potential impact on housing delivery, adding regulation and increasing risk without improving consumer protections.

“We have consistently supported strong consumer protections, accountability for your role and what you have control of in the building supply chain, and we support the development of decennial liability insurance as an important additional protection,” Ms Berry said.

“Importantly, the government has now recognised that where appropriate insurance protections are in place, there is no public policy justification for treating directors as the ultimate ‘insurer of last resort’.”

Ms Berry said the amendments demonstrated consumer protection and housing delivery did not have to be in conflict.

Planning Minister Chris Steel says LDI will protect owners corporations from costly rectifications. Photo: Claire Fenwicke.

Mr Steel said the amendments would provide a strong incentive for developers to take up LDI, which provides 10 years of protection for an owners corporation if defects are identified after a building is completed, even if the developer goes bust.

Mr Steel said that LDI would also help to prevent defects in the first place, through a rigorous inspection regime throughout the build as part of the insurer’s management of future claims liabilities.

“LDI providers engage a technical inspection service or TIS to review designs and inspect works during construction, helping to ensure that buildings are free of serious defects, prior to the policy being issued to the new building owner,” he told the Legislative Assembly.

“This TIS approach is broader in scope and deeper in detail than a standard building certification process.

“In combination, the TIS and the first resort insurance cover provided by an LDI policy further reduces the likelihood of serious defects and ensures prompt rectification.”

The legislation would kick-start the transition to LDI in the Territory and the development of compliant products, including minimum requirements and the information sharing between developers and insurers during construction.

“While this amendment will allow a developer to choose whether to take out an LDI policy or be subject to the personal liability provisions, we think that developers will choose the LDI pathway based on feedback that we have received from the market,” Mr Steel said.

“We will monitor this very carefully and the government may move to mandate LDI for these larger residential property developments in the future.”

But Master Builders ACT CEO Anna Neelagama said introducing an insurance product that did not currently exist in the ACT market would do nothing to improve building quality or prevent defects in the first place, only add yet another layer of cost for residential building in the ACT.

“There is currently only one provider of latent defects insurance in Australia. Rather than creating an artificial insurance solution, our focus should be firmly on getting buildings right during construction,” Ms Neelagama said.

‘That means better regulation, stronger oversight and effective checks and balances throughout the building process before defects occur and before consumers are left dealing with the consequences.”

Ms Neelagama said allowing developers to effectively buy their way out of their statutory responsibilities did nothing to improve accountability or deliver better outcomes for Canberrans.

“If the government is serious about improving building quality, its focus should be on a comprehensive uplift in skills and competency standards across the industry, actually delivering the long-promised trade contractor licensing regime, strengthening regulatory oversight and ensuring standards are properly enforced,” she said.

Owners Corporation Network president Gary Petherbridge said LDI redressed the imbalance in the property industry that homebuyers had long experienced.

“It’s all about increasing the amount of protection for consumers, and let’s face it, we’ve had a rough deal. It’s a good thing,” he said.

But he agreed with Ms Neelagama that the government should also extend trade licensing to areas such as waterproofing, the main source of defects.

“The major faults that have caused building defects in Canberra have been water-related membranes and on balconies and roofing,” he said.

“There’s still no licensing for those trades, and yet they’re the major reason for the defects.”

canberra.title: OpenAI hacks into Australia’s Medicare data systems
canberra.snippet: American artificial intelligence corporation OpenAI has illegally hacked into Australian Medicare data to access government files, an inc...
canberra.content:
An agent of OpenAI has hacked into Medicare’s systems, sparking alarm across Australia. Photo: Julia Gomina.

American artificial intelligence corporation OpenAI has illegally hacked into Australian Medicare data to access government files, an incident Anthony Albanese has described as extremely concerning.

An OpenAI software agent gained access three months ago, but the company has only just informed the Australian Government, and even then only via an email to a Services Australia public inbox.

The Prime Minister has let the AI giant know he is not happy with either the incident or the delay in being told about it.

Mr Albanese said he had a “frank” discussion with OpenAI’s chief executive Sam Altman, saying the company took three months to notify the government of the breach and, when it did, the notification was in an email sent to the Services Australia public inbox.

“Today I spoke with the CEO of OpenAI, Sam Altman, to express Australia’s extreme concern about this incident,” Mr Albanese said from New York on Thursday morning (Australian time).

“And I also expressed my disappointment that it took the company way too long to inform the government what had occurred, and the nature of the way that that notification occurred as well was unacceptable.”

The breach occurred on 18 June, with the OpenAI agent gaining unauthorised access to the Medicare statistics reporting service portal, which is administered by Services Australia.

Public and non-public files were accessed, but the Prime Minister says it appears no one’s personal Medicare details were accessed in the hack.

“A forensic investigation aided by the Australian Signals Directorate (ASD) is now underway to ascertain more information, including what other government systems were affected,” the PM said.

“The Medicare Statistics Reporting Portal is a public-facing statistics portal that contains non-sensitive Medicare information relating to data and statistics such as spending.

“No personal information is believed to have been accessed at this stage, but investigations are ongoing.

“Evidence currently available is that there is no broader compromise to the Services Australia network. Nonetheless, this situation is obviously unacceptable.”

A taskforce has now been set up to undertake an “urgent and immediate review” into this incident and to determine whether existing processes are appropriate to respond to AI-related cyber incidents.

The taskforce will be led by the Department of Prime Minister and Cabinet and involve the National Cybersecurity Coordinator, the Office of AI, the ASD, the Australian AI Safety Institute, and Services Australia.

It will also report on possible law enforcement and legislative responses, with the possibility of the Australian Federal Police being called in.

The incident will also be referred to Federal Parliament’s Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence.

Making matters worse, OpenAI’s vice president of global policy, Ann O’Leary, was in Canberra just last week demanding Australia loosen its copyright laws for her company, but she did not mention the Medicare data breach to anyone.

That was four days after OpenAI quietly emailed Services Australia, but a day before the agency noticed it and alerted the ASD.

Communications Minister Anika Wells said it was “highly concerning” that the company “didn’t feel obliged” to let the Federal Government know about the hack for three months.

“We want big tech to take bigger responsibility for Australians and their safety and their welfare,” she said.

Opposition Leader Angus Taylor, however, says it’s Labor that has some questions to answer over the data breach.

He said the government was not doing enough to protect system security amid new technology developments.

“A lot of our personal information is on those systems,” Mr Taylor said.

“The government needs to explain when it first became aware of the breach, exactly what information was accessed, what vulnerability was exploited, and how they’re closing it.”

Government Services Minister Katy Gallagher fronted the media in Sydney with Acting Prime Minister Richard Marles. She said she’s asking OpenAI detailed questions, including about logged information.

“The first technical exchange between OpenAI and Services Australia happened on Tuesday this week,” Senator Gallagher said.

“There are going to be subsequent meetings of those. They haven’t concluded.”

The Greens have labelled the data breach as “a serious attack on Australia’s sovereign interests” and demand the government call in new US Ambassador Dave Brat for a grilling.

“A US company linked to the Trump Administration hacking what is arguably the most valuable and sensitive database in Australia is a serious attack on Australia’s sovereignty,” acting Greens leader Mehreen Faruqi said.

“The US Ambassador must be summoned to explain what the US Government knew and what policy responses they are taking to this serious attack from a major US corporation.”

ACT independent senator David Pocock described the breach as “very concerning but ultimately unsurprising”.

“It again highlights how slow the Australian Government has been to implement appropriate safeguards for AI in high-risk settings,” he said.

“This begs the question about why the Albanese Government shelved plans for a National AI Safety Act and why they are so slow to develop legislation to implement new standards.”

australia.title: Boy, 11, shot in the face and neck in Sydney dies from his injuries
australia.snippet: The 11-year-old died at Westmead children’s hospital three days after incident at a unit in Norwest Get our breaking news email , free ap...
australia.content:
A young boy who was allegedly shot at a home in Sydney’s north-west earlier this week has died.

Police said that the boy, who had been in a critical condition since being found with a gunshot wound at a unit in Norwest on Monday, died in hospital at about 8pm on Thursday.

Police had been called to the unit in Fairway Drive at about 5pm on Monday after reports of a shooting.

Officers found the 11-year-old boy had sustained a gunshot wound to his face and neck.

He was treated at the scene by NSW Ambulance paramedics before being taken to at Westmead Children’s hospital in a critical condition.

Five other people who were in the home at the time of the incident were not injured.

Three men, all aged 18, were arrested. Two were taken to The Hills police station and later released pending further inquiries.

One of the men, Isaac Bechara, was charged with concealing a serious indictable offence, while two of the other men were arrested and released pending further inquiries.

He appeared at Blacktown local court on Tuesday morning , where he made no application for bail, which was refused.

Det Supt Naomi Moore told reporters on Tuesday afternoon that police were “aware” of the unit where the shooting had occurred and had “engaged with the occupants previously”.

“This shooting at this stage does not appear to be linked directly to current conflicts however a number of individuals who were inside the unit at the time are well known to NSW police,” she said. “Their association with organised crime is being considered by investigators.”

Police said the investigation was continuing.

australia.title: Beau Lamarre-Condon sized up surfboard bag against friend before allegedly murdering Sydney couple, court told
australia.snippet: Former NSW police officer has pleaded not guilty to murdering Jesse Baird and Luke Davies before concealing bodies in bags bought from sp...
australia.content:
Beau Lamarre-Condon was seen sizing up a surfboard bag used to dispose of a victim days before the police officer murdered two men, prosectors have alleged in a Sydney court, with chilling CCTV footage shown to the jury.

Months earlier, the 31-year-old had asked a friend over a video call to help him obtain something, and then formed a gun gesture with his hand, the NSW supreme court trial heard on Thursday.

Lamarre-Condon has been accused of fatally shooting Sydney couple Jesse Baird, 26, and Luke Davies, 29, with his police service weapon at Baird’s Paddington home on 19 February 2024.

The 31-year-old earlier this week pleaded not guilty to two counts of murder and one charge of aggravated break and enter.

CCTV footage taken from Miranda Westfield on 17 February was played to the NSW supreme court trial on Thursday showing Lamarre-Condon’s movements before the alleged murders.

In the compilation, Lamarre-Condon’s grey Tesla is seen passing by the shopping centre before the police officer and a friend enter a Decathlon store.

The pair walk straight to the surfboard bag section, where Lamarre-Condon runs his hands across the options before picking out a cover.

He holds it up and appears to measure it against his friend’s height as the other man stands straight. The bag clears his friend’s head by a few centimetres.

Watching from the pews of the Sydney courtroom, Davies and Baird’s family shook their heads as the footage was played.

During the prosecution’s openings on Monday, crown prosecutor Brett Hatfield SC alleged Lamarre-Condon asked his friend whether he would fit in the bag.

In the footage, Lamarre-Condon takes the bag to the cashier and pays for it using $90 in cash, according to receipts shown to the court.

Two days later, the police officer would allegedly shoot the two men and place Baird in the bag bought from the Westfield, the prosecution alleged.

Lamarre-Condon returned to the same store shortly after the shooting to buy a second surfboard bag to conceal Davies’ body, Hatfield said.

More than 14,000 hours of CCTV footage was obtained from 200 locations during the police investigation, the detective in charge, Sasha Pinazza, told the court.

Other videos played to the jury on Thursday showed Lamarre-Condon collecting the alleged murder weapon from a police gun locker the day before the shootings, and his mother at a car rental business picking up the vehicle he would use to drive to Baird’s house.

In footage from the morning of the alleged crime, the policeman is seen walking in the vicinity of Baird’s home before CCTV from a neighbouring house captures the sound of three gunshots.

The audio had been played during the crown’s opening remarks on Monday. But as the recording was again heard in the court room, the couple’s friends and family flinched at the sounds of the bangs.

The prosecution has told the jury that Lamarre-Condon developed an “infatuation and obsession” with Baird that manifested in compulsive behaviour during their brief relationship.

During his opening statement, Hatfield said Lamarre-Condon had misused his authority as a police officer after CCTV footage of Baird with another man at the Royal hotel in Paddington in May 2023 was allegedly found on Lamarre-Condon’s personal devices. That video was played to the jury on Wednesday and released to the media on Thursday.

His behaviour allegedly escalated after the younger man broke things off for the last time in November 2023.

An old friend of Lamarre-Condon, who used the pseudonym Alex Carrol in court, told the jury the accused called her on 23 November 2023.

They began a call before Lamarre-Condon said: “Can I ask you for something? But I can’t ask you over the phone – can we FaceTime?”

He then asked for a favour from the father of her children, referred to in court as Robert Thomas.

Carrol told the court Lamarre-Condon formed his hand into a gun and mouthed the words “can Robert get me a gun?”

She and her sister, who could see the screen, looked at each other in shock. Carrol then asked Lamarre-Condon: “Why would you ask for a gun, you’re in the police?” He shrugged off the question, the court heard.

It’s alleged Lamarre-Condon began planning to murder Baird in early 2024.

The defence team has claimed the police officer was acting in self-defence after he disguised himself as an Uber Eats driver and entered Baird’s home on the day of the shootings.

The trial before justice Natalie Adams continues.

australia.title: Second child dies after alleged Blue Mountain stabbing as mother faces additional murder charge
australia.snippet: One-year-old dies after alleged attack on Sunday, while three-year-old sibling remains in critical condition Get our breaking news email ...
australia.content:
A baby has died in a Sydney hospital five days after a mother allegedly stabbed them and two other children in the Blue Mountains, police say.

Bystanders were first on the scene after finding the three children and the 42-year-old woman with stab wounds inside a vehicle at Valley Heights in the Blue Mountains, west of Sydney, on Sunday afternoon.

A five-year-old child died at the scene, police said, despite witnesses rushing to help, delivering first aid while waiting for emergency services to arrive.

Their three-year-old and one-year-old siblings were taken to hospital with serious injuries, police said.

On Thursday evening, New South Wales police said the infant had died in hospital and the three-year-old child remained in a critical condition.

They said the woman – who was taken to Westmead hospital after the alleged attack – would face an additional charge of murder over the one-year-old’s death.

She had on Tuesday been charged with murder (DV) and two counts of causing grievous bodily harm with intent to murder.

The woman was refused bail and was to remain in custody until her next scheduled court appearance before Penrith local court on 20 November.

Officers attached to Blue Mountains police area command are investigating the alleged domestic violence under Strike Force Karelo.

Police said earlier this week that the woman had not previously come to the attention of police and that investigators were not looking for anyone else in relation to the alleged incident on Sunday.

The woman allegedly stabbed the three children at the end of a horror weekend of violence across the state, after three women were allegedly murdered inside their homes within a 12-hour period on Saturday.

australia.snippet: This blog is now closed Get our breaking news email , free app or daily news podcast More than 600 Qantas ground crew workers have begun ...
australia.content:
Victoria police confirm death of driver involved in bus crash

Victoria police have confirmed a woman died in the bus crash in Glenburn this afternoon.

The force has just issued a statement saying the driver of one of the cars involved in the collision died at the scene.

Detectives are investigating the crash, but police say they understand the bus collided with a white car and a blue Toyota on the Melba Highway near Two Hills Road about 2.40pm.

The driver of the white car died at the scene, police say, while the driver and passenger of the Toyota sustained minor injuries.

Policed say they believe there were 18 people inside the bus, including the driver. Two occupants of the bus were taken to hospital with serious injuries, two were taken to hospital with non-life-threatening injuries, and the others were treated at the scene.

  • This post has been amended. Owing to incorrect information in a police statement an earlier version misstated the gender of the person who died.
